inputs.input: "I'll take the Mill Road Wolves contract, please."
I'll take the Primer of Bolt for 120 copper, please — then set out south for Barrowford.
Then I'm off — I set out south on the road to Barrowford.
I latch the gate and come into the yard. "Guild's finest novice, at your service — your wife said you know where the wolves have been working?"
"Four wolves at the third hedge by dusk — understood. I'll take them before they take another lamb. If the work runs past dark, I'll trouble you for that barn corner."
I hold position behind the fence, staff ready, watching the treeline until one of the wolves actually steps into the open.
I cast Arcane Bolt at the wolf standing in the open by the hedge gap.
I stay behind the fence by the fallen wolf, quiet and watchful, in case the pack comes back for their dead or for me.

I leave the carcass where it lies and head up to the house to knock on Marta's door. "They've gone north for now. Might I trouble you for that barn until dawn? I'll track the other three in the morning."
"A cup warm would be kind, thank you." I take the offered kettle drink, then bed down in the barn stall and sleep until dawn.
I cross the stream and follow the wolves' tracks north from the third hedge, tracking the remaining three into the treeline.
I approach the den split slowly and quietly, staff raised, ready to cast Arcane Bolt at whatever comes out.

world.prose:
The last few paces he took slow, heel to toe over the frost-stiff bracken, staff coming up across his body with the head trained on the split. The breathing inside went on — low, even, unbothered — and the smell thickened as he closed: musk, old meat, the ammoniac bite of a place slept in for generations.

Ten paces out, the breathing stopped.

The dark of the split shifted. Then a head filled it — a gray wolf, lean, one ear ragged at the edge, its nose working the air before its eyes had even found him. It came out low and unhurried, shoulders rolling, and stood in the worn smooth patch at the den mouth with its head no higher than his knee. Behind it, deeper in the rock, a second shape moved — a gleam of eyes, the scrape of claws on stone, staying.

The one before him looked at the staff. At him. Its lips came off its teeth by slow degrees, not a snarl yet, more a showing of the account: the light-stick, the crack like the sky splitting, the big one that had not come home. Its hackles rose in a ridge from neck to tail, and it stepped sideways — one step, two — angling, putting a fallen slab of rock between itself and him while it kept its face turned to him.

From the split behind it came a second growl now, deeper, and the ragged-eared one's own voice joined it, rumbling up out of its chest, and the sound of it filled the little hollow of the rocks from all sides at once.

The staff's head hummed against his palm, the bolt gathering at its tip and wanting out, and three yards of frost-bitten ground stood between him and the first set of bared teeth.

I approach the den split slowly and quietly, staff raised, ready to cast Arcane Bolt at whatever comes out.

I leave the den and walk the Mill Road treeline to look for the other wolves, keeping the den for last.

world.prose:
He stepped past the dead wolf — its fur cold now, frost beginning on the stiff hairs of its ragged ear — and took the treeline north, the way the pack's traffic had worn the ground. And worn it was: the leaf litter here was beaten into a ribbon of packed earth winding along the rockface, wide as a cart track in places, studded with prints. Not old ones. The edges of the presses still held their sharpness, mud squeezed up in the middle of each pad, and last night's melt had not yet dried in the deepest of them.

The trail ran ahead of him through the thin trees, and a hundred yards on it told him more. The prints split at a leaning birch — two sets of tracks, two wolves by the spacing, turning off east down a slope toward the sound of water, their stride long and unhurried. The wider ribbon went on north, pressed deep and used often, and from somewhere down that northern line, faint on the cold air, came a smell the dead den's musk had masked until now: old kill. Rot and wet hide, somewhere off among the trunks.

He marked the birch and kept to the main trail, working the treeline as he'd meant to, den held behind him. The woodpecker fell silent. A jay did not. And then the trees thinned ahead into a hollow where the ground dipped to a stony runoff channel, and there — not fifty paces off, on the far side of the channel with its back to him — stood a wolf.

Big through the shoulder, gray going to white at the muzzle, head lowered over something dark in the stones. It was feeding. The wind sat still between them, and the channel's babble covered his steps, and for this moment it had not marked him at all: fifty paces of open dip and thin trees, one wolf in the light, and the trail it had come from visible behind it, winding off north toward that old-kill smell.

inputs.input: I cast Arcane Bolt at the charging gray-muzzled wolf.
I throw another stone into the den split to flush out whatever's still inside, standing ready at Medium range.
I lower my staff and back away from the den, leaving the female and her pups alive, then head back up the shepherd track to find the boy.

I tell the boy the gray-muzzled leader is dead, along with several others from the pack, and that I left the den mother and her pups alive. "The big gray one is taken care of, and most of the pack with him — your sheep should graze that cor
"That's me. The road wolves are next — where along the Mill Road have they been hitting the flocks, and when?"
"A dip by the beck and the broken wall at dusk — I'll be there before evening. You can tell your father the gray one is dead and the road wolves are next."
I head down the shepherd track toward the mill and the beck dip, planning to reach the broken wall well before evening.
I find a shaded spot near the broken wall with a clear view of the dip and the hazels, settle in to wait, and meditate to recover MP until dusk approaches.
I keep watch from my spot by the broken wall through the night, staff ready, watching the dip and the hazels for the road wolves.

Two nights and no wolves have shown at the dip — I head back to Barrowford, to the shepherd's house, third past the mill with the blue door, and knock to ask his father where the road wolves are actually ranging.
"Thank you. North end of the treeline, by the low wall, at evening or first light — I'll be there tonight and see your flocks safe."
I spend the day preparing, then head to the north end of the treeline by the low wall in the afternoon to find a good hidden spot before the wolves come an hour or two after dark.

t90.prose:
The day's preparing was plain work: a meal and a rest at the inn, the staff's head wiped clean, a fresh strip of cloth around the old knot on the shaft where his grip had worn it, and a long hour in the yard behind the smithy testing the bolt-cast until his hands remembered the pull of it. He bought nothing, spoke to nobody who wanted more than the time of day, and was on the east lane out of Barrowford before the sun stood high.

The north end of the treeline was a different country from the dip. Here the hazels and older ash ran right down to the grass, just as the shepherd had said, and the wall along the pasture's edge sank from hip height to a knee-high tumble of stones overgrown with moss and bramble. Sheep grazed the far side of the pasture with a dog sprawled near them, and they gave the treeline a wide, deliberate berth, cropping in a band that stopped a dozen paces short of the wall as if a rope were strung there.

He worked the ground slowly, and the ground paid him. Behind the low wall's worst collapse the bramble grew in a deep waist-high bank, and inside the bank the sheep themselves had worn a dry, sheltered hollow where the stems arched overhead — a place a man could sit out of the wind with the wall's stones at his front and a clean view through a gap in the bramble across the whole near grass, the low wall, and the first dark ranks of the trees. From it he could see everything a wolf would have to cross and be seen by nothing until it was too late. He cleared a few dead stems from the gap with his hands, tested the sight-line, and settled in.

The afternoon went long and slow. The light leaned, reddened, and went; the flock bunched and settled with the dog among them; a bat began its crooked work over the grass. The cold came up the same as last night, the dew the same. Once, an hour into the dark, something far down the treeline cracked a branch — one sharp sound, no second — and the pasture held its breath and then went on breathing. He stayed in the hollow, staff across his knees, watching the gap.

The moon rose thin and late. Past it, well into the true dark, the flock stirred in its sleep — a low, rolling unease, sheep rising and standing — and the dog came up off its belly with its head high, nose into the wind, and held still that way, listening, looking east toward the trees.
